sentences.text: Paracathartes was a paleognathous bird, a group that includes modern ostriches and tinamous, possessing a turkey-like stature and size that closely resembled a tinamou.
Remarkably, nearly complete skeletons from at least five individuals were preserved together in a single find.
Fossils associated with the species include three whole eggs and an avian neurocranium, a skull case that may belong to Paracathartes or a large predatory bird.
The holotype, the specimen the species is based on, is cataloged as ROM 22658 in the Royal Ontario Museum and consists of the distal end of a left tibiotarsus, a lower leg bone.
This specimen was collected by G. E. Lindblad and G. Sternberg on August 4, 1949.
Further fossils were found at the northernmost branch of Elk Creek near Basin, Wyoming.
Unlike other lithornithids, Paracathartes was likely a poor flyer, similar to its modern relatives.
Houde classified Paracathartes as a member of the order Lithornithiformes and family Lithornithidae in 1988, identifying the family Lithornithidae as the parent group for the genus.
Paracathartes lived during the Greybullian, middle Wasatchian, and Ypresian stages, approximately 56 to 48.07 million years ago, within the Willwood Formation of the Bighorn Basin.
Harrison originally described Paracathartes as the earliest known vulture of the Cathartidae family, but Rich criticized this assignment, arguing against placing the genus within the vulture family.
